claims.text: The ductility of Ti-6Al-4V is attributable to its dual-phase alpha-beta microstructure.
The alpha phase has an HCP crystal structure.
The HCP alpha phase provides a high degree of slip-system activation.
The beta phase has a BCC crystal structure.
The beta phase facilitates strain hardening through the formation of dislocation networks.
The combined strain hardening and slip-system activation of the alpha and beta phases enhances ductility.
Annealed Ti-6Al-4V has equiaxed alpha grains.
Annealed Ti-6Al-4V has a uniform distribution of beta phase.
The proposed tensile testing uses a strain rate of 0.001 s^-1 over 20-400 degrees Celsius.
The alpha and beta phases enable dislocation movement.
The alpha and beta phases enable grain-boundary sliding under the stated conditions.
Ti-6Al-4V will have 20% greater elongation at break than pure titanium.
Ti-6Al-4V will have an elongation at break of 15% ± 2%.
Pure titanium has an elongation at break of 12% ± 1.5%.
Ductility below 10% indicates inadequate strain hardening and slip-system activation.
A 10% elongation threshold is generally the minimum acceptable ductility for titanium alloys in structural applications.
Variations in microstructure and material properties contribute to uncertainty in the predicted ductility.
A measured elongation below 9% would show that the dual-phase microstructure does not provide sufficient strain hardening and slip-system activation.

contradictions.description: An increase from the stated 12% baseline to the stated 15% prediction is a 25% relative increase, not the claimed 20% increase.
The intervention specifies testing over 20-400°C, whereas the conditions characterize operation as ambient temperature; most of the stated testing range is not ambient.

The hypothesis predicts improvement over a 12% pure-titanium baseline, but the falsification rule only rejects results below 9%; results from 9% through 12% would fail to show the claimed improvement without falsifying the hypothesis.
